sessions.what: We did not summarise the marketing. Nextify.ai gave us Pro access for this test — disclosed here and in the video that goes with this review — and nothing else was agreed: no copy approval, and no draft shared before publication. On 7 September 2026 we generated a real ad from a product image inside that account, read the credit cost the app charges for every model it offers, and checked the pricing page both signed in and signed out. Everything below is what the product did and charged, not what the site says it does.
findings: Credits are charged per second of output, not per video. A four-second 720p clip on Seedance 2.0 — the model the editor pre-selects — cost 48 credits and took the balance from 3,000 to 2,952. The app's own credit table prices that combination at 12 a second, and the Generate button reads 48 before you commit, so the arithmetic is visible if you know to look for it.

Every tier's video count assumes 20 credits a video. Starter's 1,000 credits are sold as 50 videos, Pro's 3,000 as 150 and Business's 8,000 as 400 — all exactly 20 apiece, which is four seconds on the cheapest 5-credit-a-second model. On the model the editor actually opens with, Pro is 62 clips; at the 15-second maximum it is 16.

No image model costs what the image counts assume. Those counts work out at 2 credits an image on every tier, including the free one. The cheapest image model in the table is Nano Banana 2 at 1k for 7 credits, and the pre-selected GPT Image 2 is 10 — the button literally reads “Generate Image 10”. Starter's “up to 500 images” is about 100.

The avatar tools are the expensive ones, and they are the reason most people arrive. UGC Product Video and Lip-sync run on HeyGen AV4 at 6.7 credits a second, identical at 720p and 1080p, over 3 to 120 seconds. A 30-second avatar ad is 201 credits and a 60-second one is 402, so a Pro month is fourteen or seven of them.

Free users cannot reach the Seedance models at all. The model configuration marks seedance-2.0, seedance-2.0-fast and seedance-2.0-mini as unavailable on the free plan, so the 50 free credits run on Kling or MiniMax with a watermark — about two three-second clips.

“In seconds” is not what happens, but “three minutes” is fair. Our four-second clip took 126 seconds from submit to finished file, against the app's own on-screen estimate of four minutes. The homepage claim “Product Image to Viral Ad in 3 Minutes” holds up; the “in seconds” line on the same page does not.

The output was accurate to the prompt. We asked for a stainless steel insulated bottle on a kitchen counter in morning light, a hand picking it up, clean styling and no text overlay, and that is what came back — 9:16, 720p, four seconds, with generated audio. Nothing in the result argued against the tool; the argument is with the pricing page.
The pricing page hides the free plan once you sign in. Signed out, Free sits at the head of the ladder; signed in, the same URL starts at Starter.

sessions.what: Daan created the free account and logged in; everything after that was read inside the workspace on 11 September 2026 -- the credit screen, the plans and billing screen and the upgrade panel -- alongside Bitscale's own credit documentation. Two limits worth stating plainly. We did not run an enrichment: the grid renders in a canvas our browser panel could not drive, so the per-record credit costs below come from Bitscale's published credit table and not from a meter we moved ourselves. And Bitscale is an affiliate partner of ours; their partner manager offered 2,000 bonus credits that same morning, which had not been added when we looked -- the account was on the ordinary free allowance of 200, which is what a new reader gets.
findings: The free tier runs two meters, not one, and the account screen shows both: 200 platform credits and 2,000 search credits, each resetting monthly, with the next search reset dated on the page. Enriching a record spends platform credits; finding one through Find People or Find Companies spends a search credit, one per record. A reader budgeting on "200 credits" is reading half the meter, and it is the half that runs out first.

On Free, nothing carries over. The billing screen states it twice -- "Rolled-Over Credits: Not included in the plan" and "Rollover Limit: Not included in the plan" -- so an unused month is gone rather than banked. Rollover is listed among the things the first paid plan unlocks, next to credit rollover, the 100+ providers, action columns beyond 20 per grid, and the inbound integrations (RB2B, Factors, Vector).

What one enriched record costs is published, and the range is the whole story: one to twelve platform credits per successful email or phone lookup, depending on how many providers the waterfall is allowed to try. An AI enrichment is one to two credits a run, a BitAgent website scrape one per query, and anything arriving through the API is free. On Growth that turns 15,000 credits into anywhere between 1,250 and 15,000 enriched contacts -- 2.3 cents each at one credit, 28 cents at twelve.

The in-app upgrade panel carries a Growth benefit the public plan cards do not mention: three hours a quarter with a GTM engineer, alongside the 15,000 credits. Worth knowing before you compare the $349 against a pure data vendor, because it is consulting time rather than volume.

The two meters are set to become convertible. Bitscale's documentation announces 1 platform credit = 10 search credits as an upcoming feature, handled manually for enterprise accounts today. Until that ships, a month where you burn the enrichment pool cannot be topped up from the search pool, however much of it is left.

sessions.what: We did not read the docs and summarise them: PartnerStack is the platform our own affiliate operation runs on. We manage 58 partner programmes through it, pull the Partner API v2 on a schedule, and stamp sub-IDs across 704 pages of our own site. PartnerStack is also an affiliate partner of ours — we earn 15% of every sale for a year on anyone who signs up through our link — which is why the findings below are things we measured against our own records rather than claims from their marketing.
findings: A record in the customers endpoint is a tracked click, not a signup. One plain curl on a tracking link produced a customer record one second later, has_paid false, with no browser and no account. Records surface in the API about five minutes after the click, so allow ten before concluding a test did nothing.

Clicks arrive without a source. There is no referring-URL field in the partnership data, so the platform can tell you a link was clicked and never which page produced it. We had to build sub-ID stamping across our own pages to answer that question ourselves.

Commission terms do not come from the API. offers.base_rate is returned null on every partnership we hold. The readable source is PartnerStack's own public directory at market.partnerstack.com — and it sometimes contradicts the vendor's own affiliate page, which is worth knowing before you quote a rate to anyone.

Programme status lags the reality by days. One partner sent us a welcome email with a working tracking link on 7 August; the API still read application-denied and only turned active somewhere between 13 and 18 August. Treat the vendor's email as the leading indicator and the API status as the one that catches up.
The earned-commission endpoints are the weakest part. rewards and transactions did not return usable data for us, so what you have actually been paid is a dashboard question rather than an API one.

Partner replies break email threading. A partner answers inside the PartnerStack dashboard and the platform sends that on as a fresh message from hello@partnerstackmail.com, with a new Message-ID and no reference to the mail it is answering. Any automation of yours that matches replies to threads will not match these.

sessions.what: We did not stop at the marketing. On 25 September 2026 we opened a free Jibble account (organisation 'AIBM hands-on test', web browser only), clocked in and out, invited a second user, exported a timesheet and opened the upgrade screen without buying anything. Nothing was agreed with Jibble about this test. Everything below is what the product did and showed, not what the site says.
findings: The account lands on Free at €0, marked as the selected plan, with a 14-day trial of the paid features running alongside it. During those two weeks nothing is locked, so what you see in week one is more than Free keeps.

The price table exists, just not on the public site. The upgrade button opens four plans with annual and monthly prices (euros, excluding VAT, as shown from the Netherlands): Free €0; Essentieel €1.79 or €2.99; Groei €3.79 or €4.99; Pro €6.79 or €9.29 per user a month. No demo form and no sales call in between.

Jibble's own plan comparison, one click further, answers what Free excludes: no timesheet approval workflow, no automatic break deductions or custom pay periods, no smart reminders, alerts or automatic clock-out, no groups, one admin, two locations, one work schedule and one kiosk, and no attendance report, leave workflow or leave balances. Free keeps overtime calculations, face recognition, selfie, PIN and NFC clock-ins, GPS-verified clock-ins and geofences, timesheet and report exports, and the Slack, Microsoft Teams, QuickBooks Online, Xero, Deel and Zapier integrations.
Setting up the organisation requires a phone number; the form will not continue without one. The marketing opt-in on the sign-up form is ticked by default.
Clocking out in the same minute you clocked in is refused, with a message saying you cannot clock out before clocking in. Jibble records whole minutes; two minutes later it worked.
Inviting a second member took a name and an email address and went through without any prompt to pay. The member shows as pending until they accept.

The weekly timesheet export offers XLS or CSV. Our CSV arrived within seconds and carries 32 columns per member per day, including worked hours, paid and unpaid breaks, deductions, payroll hours, daily and weekly overtime and billable amounts.
We did not switch on face recognition or GPS. The comparison puts both in Free; anti-spoofing, device lock and live location tracking are Pro only.

sessions.what: Daan started the 30-day trial; everything after that was measured inside the account. The first question the protocol asked was whether the trial takes a card, because their pricing page does not say. It does not — but the answer is on the signup page, not the pricing page, which is a small lesson in where vendors put the reassuring sentence.
findings: No card for the trial. The signup page states it plainly — “Try it free for 30 days. No credit card required. Cancel anytime.” — and the form asks only for an email address and a password. The pricing page, where you would actually look, says nothing about it.

The prices inside the account are not the prices on the pricing page. The public page leads with the promotional rate, currently a limited-time 90% off for three months. The in-app upgrade screen quotes the real thing: Lite $23, Plus $43, Premium $70 a month, with a Yearly toggle marked “Save 10%”. Sign up on the strength of $2.30 and the first screen you see afterwards is $23.
Two add-ons ride along on every tier, and they are easy to miss: Team Members at $11 per user a month, and Advanced Payments at $20 a month. They are listed under Lite, Plus and Premium alike.

Removing FreshBooks branding from the emails your client receives is not a paid feature — it is a quote-only one. It appears only on the top “Let's Talk” tier, alongside lower card fees and two included team members. On Lite, Plus and Premium your invoice mail carries their brand.

The client ceiling that decides the tier is not testable during the trial. Lite stops at 5 clients, Plus at 50, Premium unlimited — but the trial runs with full features, as the upgrade screen says in as many words (“Upgrade to a paid plan to continue using all of FreshBooks' great features”). We fed the client importer a six-client CSV and it accepted the file and moved straight to field matching, with no limit warning at the point where a Lite account would have stopped. So the meter that will actually bite you is the one you cannot feel while you are evaluating.
Prices are shown in USD on a Netherlands account, and the plan screen carries the note “Features vary by region.”

sessions.what: We already knew from their pricing pages that Glide sells two products. What we had never done is the thing a reader does: go to glideapps.com and press the free signup button. Daan created the account; everything after that was measured in the product.
findings: The free signup button does not lead to the product our pricing section describes. Both “Sign up” and “Get started” on glideapps.com point at os.glideapps.dev — GlideOS. We signed up and landed there. The classic builder, with the free tier of unlimited drafts, one editor and 25k rows, sits behind glideapps.com/classic, which you only reach if you already know to look for it.

The two ladders are an order of magnitude apart. Classic business pricing starts at $199 a month billed yearly; GlideOS Basic is $25 a month. Same brand, same homepage, two different products with two different price floors.

And the meter is different. Classic bills updates — 5,000 included, 2 cents each after that. GlideOS bills credits: Basic 100 a month, Plus 250, Pro 500 and upward with team size. So the “updates, not seats” warning that applies to Classic does not describe the product a new signup actually lands in.

GlideOS's free tier publishes no number. Every paid tier lists its credit allowance; the free column says “Limited credits”, alongside 2 team members and 10 projects. Nowhere in the app is there a balance — not on the dashboard, not in the account menu, not on the upgrade screen. You cannot find out what you have or what you have spent.

The AI itself is not walled off on free. From one sentence — “build a simple app to track software subscriptions” — it drew up a plan, asked a sensible clarifying question about where the data lives today, produced a working mockup and then began importing components one by one. We hit no credit wall during any of it.

sessions.what: Two sessions on the free plan. On 7 September we ran it by hand: Daan logged in, and we read every counter against a test file of exactly five minutes that we built inside the page; Descript was not a partner of ours then and contributed nothing. On 30 September, by then a PartnerStack partner, we drove Descript from Claude through Descript's connector, for Descript's partner content challenge, which pays the first five entries $250: we uploaded one of our own five-minute review videos and asked for vertical clips in plain sentences, once directly and once from a claude.ai chat.
findings: The free plan's 100 AI credits are one-time, not monthly. Descript says so itself in two places: the plan card reads "100 AI credits at signup" for Free against "400 AI credits / month" for Hobbyist, and the usage screen inside the app puts "Lifetime AI credits used 0/100" next to "Monthly media minutes used 0/60". That pair of words -- lifetime against monthly -- is the whole answer.

Media minutes come off at IMPORT, not at export, and per minute of media. Two five-minute files took the counter from 60m to 50m. Their own upload dialog says it too: "Each file added uses media minutes". Exporting costs no minutes and no credits, according to Descript itself.

The AI assistant, Underlord, charges per instruction, and it does run on the free plan. Importing and transcribing cost 3 credits, Studio Sound over a ten-minute track 9 credits, and a question about the export settings 6 credits.

An instruction that returns nothing still costs credits. "Remove all filler words" answered "No filler words were found -- the script shows 0 words, so there's nothing to remove" and deducted 2 credits anyway.
Five instructions without a single real edit spent 20 of the 100 one-time credits. Anyone using the free plan as a trial is through it in an afternoon, and no more arrive.

Studio Sound ran on Free, while the pricing table presents it as a Hobbyist benefit ("Studio Sound, Remove Filler Words, Create Clips, and more"). The line "Limited use of Underlord" on the free card is therefore more generous than the comparison table suggests.
In onboarding, the consent "Our team analyzes your project information" is TICKED BY DEFAULT, in a step most people click straight through. You can turn it off, but you have to do it yourself.

A row with only the Organisation column filled does build a company record on its own. Our “Solitary Holdings BV” row arrived as an organisation with its phone number attached.

But “overwrite” means exactly the four fields it names — name, job title, organisation and custom fields — and nothing else. The two rows carried different phone numbers and the contact now holds BOTH, sitting side by side. Contact channels are appended, not replaced, so a bad update pass leaves duplicate numbers on the record rather than wrong ones.

There is no undo, and that is worth knowing before you press Import. The import history logs “34 total imported, 34 contacts created” and offers exactly two things: View and Close. View opens a saved filter holding precisely those 34 contacts — which looks like the undo route until you select all of them and find the only bulk actions are Tag, Create Campaign and Export. No delete. Not on that list, not on the full contact list, not on the contact record, and not on its edit screen. We could not reach a delete anywhere in the interface.
So the practical rule is the opposite of reassuring: an import is one-way. Test on a handful of rows first, because the clean-up you are counting on does not exist where you would look for it.

sessions.what: Historical test data: these are measurements from 4 September 2026, at that day's free allowance and meters, not today's Free plan or the standard cost of every Bot. We ran the reproducible test BrowserAct's own partner team proposed, on a free account with the 1,500 sign-up credits the card offered at the time. The prompt, verbatim: open books.toscrape.com, collect the first 20 books in listing order, open each detail page and return full title, displayed price, availability and source URL, leave unavailable fields blank, infer nothing. Before touching BrowserAct we fetched the same 20 pages with plain HTTP and saved the four fields as ground truth, so every value below was checked against the source, not against BrowserAct's own claims. Then we built the Bot from the prompt, ran it twice from the published version, and read the credit meter after each step.
findings: Accuracy: 80 of 80 fields correct, three times over. The build's own verification output, run 1 and run 2 each returned 20 rows with title, price, availability and URL identical to our ground truth, including the parenthetical stock counts ('In stock (22 available)') and the currency symbol, which the Bot kept as displayed rather than converting.

The build costs more than the runs. Building the Bot took 4 minutes 59 seconds and 278 credits; the agent inspected the listing and a detail page, wrote a small package (a SKILL.md, a run.py and two DOM helpers), compiled it, and ran it end to end before declaring it ready. On that day's free tier that was about a fifth of the sign-up credits spent before the first real run. The pricing page now estimates 300 to 500 credits for a simple Agent build, and today's free card lists 2 free Agent Builds alongside its 200 credits.

Runs are cheap but not deterministic in cost. Run 1 used 21 credits in 1 minute 56 seconds; run 2, the same Bot on the same 20 pages, used 27 credits in 3 minutes 12 seconds. Identical output, 29% more credits and 65% more wall time. At Basic's 10,000 credits for $13 a month on yearly billing, a run of this size is roughly three cents, so the variance is small in money and worth knowing about in budgeting.

The meter is honest at the account level and confusing at the task level. Balance went 1,500 to 1,222 after the build, 1,201 after run 1 and 1,174 after run 2, which reconciles exactly with the per-task figures in the history list. But the task detail panel showed 'Credits used: 0' for a run that the history list, seconds later, priced at 21. Trust the list and the balance, not the panel.

The agent made one silent design decision. The prompt said 'the first 20 books', and the Bot was built with no parameters and 'first 20' hard-coded; it says so in its own summary and offers to change it on request. Fine for this test, but a Bot you intend to reuse should be built with the count as an input, and you have to ask for that.

Historical: on 4 September the app and the website showed different prices. On first login the app opened a '7-days free trial' panel listing Basic at $16, Essential at $70 and Advanced at $120 a month, with $20, $100 and $200 struck through, while the public pricing page, read the day before, still charged $20, $100 and $200 monthly. That gap closed by 13 September: the public page now shows the same $16, $70 and $120.

What this test does not show. books.toscrape.com is a static sandbox with no login, no JavaScript rendering and no anti-bot measures, so none of the managed-browser, proxy or CAPTCHA infrastructure in BrowserAct's pitch was exercised. It proves the no-code loop from plain prompt to reusable Bot; it says nothing about hostile sites, where proxy use starts to matter -- free in the cloud for a limited time, 5,000 credits per gigabyte of dynamic proxy traffic on the Local CLI.

sessions.what: On 26 September 2026 we built the same class-booking web app in Lovable, Replit and Emergent from one identical prompt, each on its free plan, and checked every result against 18 tests we wrote down before the first build. We changed no code: the builder only got our prompt. Lovable paid us nothing when we ran the test; it accepted us into its affiliate programme on 28 September 2026, and these findings were recorded before that.
findings: Lovable built and published the app in about ten minutes and used 4 of the 10 credits on a new account. It asked twice, to create the project and to publish, and published to a lovable.app address that stays online on the free plan with an 'Edit with Lovable' badge.

It was the only one of the three whose first version held the limit when ten people booked an eight-spot class at the same moment: eight accepted, two refused with 'Sorry, this class is full.' The other two accepted all ten.

It checked input on the server as well as in the form (a name of only spaces and a bad email were refused), kept the admin password out of the page and scripts, and prefixed CSV values starting with = + - or @ so a spreadsheet does not run them as formulas.
It needed no repair round. After republishing, every test booking was still there.

Taking the code with you works, taking the running app does not. With GitHub connected (access limited to one repository), Lovable created its own repository with the full source and database migrations and committed no secret keys. Outside Lovable, on Node 22, it installed and built without errors, but loaded no classes: the database service key and admin password stay in Lovable, so moving means setting up your own database and bringing the bookings as a CSV or Lovable's full database export.
sessions.not_tested: One run on one day on the free plan. Not a security audit or a load test, we did not measure how fast the 20 monthly Cloud credits run down, and we did not trigger Lovable's full database export.
